_comment: agent 站 52 份档案的「适合与不适合」英文（sec.fit → .td-fit）。2026-10-04 建；2026-10-08 A6.1 扩至 52 份。
_critical: ⚠ 这是全站最敏感的一段内容 —— 它直接告诉用户「什么该用它、什么不该用」。译错会误导选型。因此：
_rules: 0) **保留「不适合」的强度**：原文用「直接排除」「这一层也没有合适的」的地方，英文同样用 rule out / nothing here fits，不要软化成 considerations。
1) **保留未核验标记**：「本次未核验」「记为未知」「官方未公开」→ unverified / recorded as unknown / not disclosed。**这些是本站的立场，磨平它们等于伪造确定性。**
2) 保留 ** 强调与换行结构（适合/不适合 的分段是内容的一部分）。
3) 产品名、参数（-ngl、skipGitRepoCheck、YOLO 模式、Memory MCP）与能力名原样保留。
4) 「不适合」里给出的**替代方案**（用 X SDK / 走 Y 路线）必须保留 —— 那是给用户的可执行建议。
_format: 值为 Markdown 片段：先列适合项，空行后 **Not a fit for** 段落。
aider-cli:
Scenarios where AI changes must stay in git version control, diffable and revertible.
Users who need to connect local models or several cloud providers.

**Not a fit for** scenarios needing a new model release or relying on upstream fixes — the latest release stopped at 2025-08 and maintenance status is maintenance.
aider:
People who work in whatever editor they like and refuse to move to a dedicated agent interface.
People who want lightweight interaction: add a comment, get a response.

**Not a fit for** scenarios requiring strict approval — the confirmation mechanism in watch mode was not verified this round, and a resident process makes unconfirmed changes more likely.
Also not a fit for cloud background execution; it depends on a local process.
claude-code-cli:
Users who value permission control, want the MCP ecosystem, and want Anthropic's own models.
Users who want update notifications (this entry ships its own Atom feed).

**Not a fit for** scenarios needing an open-source licence, self-hosting or closed distribution — the licence is explicitly proprietary, and public source is not the same as free use.
claude-code:
People already in an IDE who want Claude without switching tools.
People who want one tool across terminal, IDE and GitHub.
People who care about permission control and the MCP ecosystem.

**Not a fit for** scenarios needing an open-source licence or self-hosting — the licence is explicitly proprietary.
Also not a fit where permission behaviour must be strictly identical between IDE and CLI; this round did not verify whether they match.
cline:
Users who need one tool across editor, terminal and desktop.
People who need model choice (not locked to one vendor).
People who need CI/CD integration (CLI headless).
People who need reviewable, revertible changes — every edit appears as a diff plus a checkpoint to undo wholesale.
People who need periodic automation (cron scheduling that survives restarts).

**Not a fit for** requiring approval to behave identically across all forms — the extension form confirms human-in-the-loop, but behaviour under CLI headless was not verified.
codex-cli:
Engineering work in the terminal, including CI integration or building your own client.
Its architecture emphasises resumption and recovery of existing repositories.
codex-ide:
A fit for two groups:

- People already in VS Code / Cursor / Windsurf who want Codex in the same environment without switching tools
- People who need the IDE and the CLI to share sessions (the app server architecture)

**Not a fit for** people who need a standalone editor — this form must attach to an existing editor and cannot be used alone.

Also note: local tasks depend on the editor process staying alive, so "keep running after shutdown" requires cloud delegation (Codex Cloud).
copilot:
People already inside the GitHub ecosystem (working via PR / Issue / Actions).
People who need the widest editor coverage (VS Code / JetBrains / Eclipse / Xcode).
Organisations that need quota-pool governance and admin spend controls.

**Not a fit for** anyone requiring pricing stated once and clearly — this round could not confirm the price figures tier by tier; check the official site yourself.
Also not a fit if you rely on third-party agent delegation (officially marked Preview).
crush:
Several kinds of people fit:

- Users who like the Charm ecosystem's terminal experience (TUI aesthetics and interaction)
- People who need to switch between several providers, or want the official Hyper subscription
- **People who want to switch models mid-session without losing context** (the official README promises exactly this)
- People who want local models and want to declare their context window explicitly
- People who need all three MCP transports supported

**Not a fit for** scenarios needing a clear open-source licence for redistribution — GitHub reports NOASSERTION and the terms were not verified.
cursor:
People who want a cloud agent that keeps running when they close the laptop.
People who need long-horizon (months) context retention and large-scale sub-agent orchestration.
**Companies whose code must not leave their own infrastructure** (the self-hosted form).

**Not a fit for** anyone requiring pricing transparent enough to compare directly — the official quota multipliers (1x / 3x / 20x) are given as multiples only, with no concrete request or token figures.
gemini-cli:
Three scenarios fit:

- You want a quick trial without installing anything (npx leaves no install footprint)
- You need MCP extensions, especially wiring Gemini's multimodal generation (Imagen / Veo / Lyria) into an agent workflow
- You need scripted non-interactive runs, for example in CI

Three kinds of people also fit:

- Anyone who needs a large context window — 1M tokens, one of the few in this track that states a limit
- Anyone who needs a revert guarantee — shadow Git checkpoints plus `/restore`
- Anyone who needs a project-level long-term instruction file — GEMINI.md

**Not a fit for** treating quota as unlimited.
The free tier has clear daily limits: 6,000 code requests + 240 chats/day.
And CLI and agent-mode quota are counted together.
grok-bot:
**A fit if you pick tools by job to be done.** The official list of nine jobs is usable directly as selection criteria (see the tools field): sales leads, site building, inbox and subscription cleanup, customer service, game assets, office scheduling, inbox, meeting attendance, refund follow-up.

**Not a fit for four kinds of people:**

- Anyone who needs a checkable, configurable approval mechanism — this entry's most obvious weakness
- Anyone who needs local file read/write
- Anyone who needs to confirm the underlying model — the official pages do not name it
- Non-English-speaking users — the official pages only name platforms (desktop and iOS), with **no country list**
opencode:
Users who need switchable multiple providers and who care about confirmation before bash commands run.
Participants in the ACP ecosystem.

**Not a fit for** fully unattended automation — asking before each command interrupts the flow; the exact switch for YOLO mode was not verified.
windsurf:
People who want a choice of model providers rather than being locked to one.
People who need ACP to attach a custom agent (note it is preview).
People who need remote host support (SSH / WSL).

**Not a fit for** paying for one editing feature alone — the Free tier already includes unlimited inline edits and unlimited Tab completion.
zed:
Scenarios where editor performance (Rust), syntactic parsing accuracy (Tree-sitter) and multi-user collaboration matter.
**Users who want to mix the native agent with external CLI agents in one editor** — this is its most distinctive value.

**Not a fit for** people looking for an editor whose only selling point is built-in AI — Zed positions itself as an orchestration layer for agents, not as "I ship my own model".
Also not a fit if you need hands-on measurements of large-repository behaviour — the indexing strategy is not publicly documented.
claude-agent-sdk:
**One line: it is a coding agent that has already been polished.**

**Swapping models and shaping the agent loop are the two things it cannot do.**

**Fits**:

- you want a coding agent that has already been polished — tool set, permission chain, hooks and session fork all included
- your team works in Python
- you are happy handing reasoning entirely to Claude

**Not a fit**:

- you need a different model / self-hosted weights — **ruled out outright**
- you need a framework-level custom agent loop — the loop shape is decided by Claude Code
- you need multi-agent orchestration — it has no first-class agents-as-tools delegation
codex-sdk:
**A good fit in four cases:**

- You want to put Codex inside your own Node app, Electron app or CI
- You need non-interactive execution
- You need file-level permission rules
- You are on a TypeScript or Python stack, have settled on OpenAI models, but want the model layer swappable

**Not a fit in two cases:**

- You want a pure library and do not want to carry a spawned CLI child process — use the OpenAI Agents SDK instead
- Your target directory is not a Git repository and you do not want to pass `skipGitRepoCheck`

⚠ One more capability boundary: **if you need a compaction API exposed at the SDK layer, it does not have one.**
The CLI side has `compact_prompt` / `experimental_compact_prompt_file` plus `PreCompact` / `PostCompact` hooks, but the SDK layer has no dedicated compaction interface — config pass-through is the only route.
crewai:
**Fits**: tasks that can be expressed as "a team with defined roles" (Crews); business logic that stays in ordinary Python with explicit control over the execution path (Flows); running on local models (the official docs name Ollama and LM Studio); needing MCP and A2A; a Python stack.

**Not a fit**: requiring process- or container-level sandboxing, or network access control — the official docs provide no such mechanism, guardrails only validate task output, and file tools are confined to `base_dir`; needing working memory and long-term memory managed separately — CrewAI has unified them into one `Memory` class, the opposite of LangGraph's split design; needing a genuinely vendor-hosted background — it is a pure library, so you deploy it to your own server or VPC.
deepagents:
**Fits**: you want a general agent that works out of the box, is tuned by default, and targets long multi-step tasks.
You do not want to assemble filesystem, memory and sub-agents yourself. You are already in the LangChain ecosystem.

**Not a fit**: needing fine-grained permission guardrails — the official docs state these are not provided, so you must build your own sandbox.
Needing strict control of the agent loop shape — use a custom LangGraph graph.
Wanting a lightweight harness — use LangChain `create_agent`.
google-adk:
**Fits**: organising multiple agents into deterministic flows with branches, loops and human intervention; defining agents and tools code-first so they are testable and versionable; a team inside the Google ecosystem (Cloud Run / Vertex / Gemini); needing built-in eval and a development UI; wanting one framework across Python and TypeScript; needing tool-level human confirmation, session persistence and resume.
**Not a fit**: running a single agent with no graph structure (OpenAI Agents SDK or Deep Agents are lighter); needing built-in file- or network-sandbox boundaries — **the official docs provide none**, so file access goes through the Artifacts abstraction or a tool you wire up yourself; wanting self-hosted weights out of the box without going through the LiteLLM adaptor layer.
hermes-agent:
**A fit for these six cases.**

- A **resident cross-platform personal assistant** (six platforms: Telegram / Discord / Slack / WhatsApp / Signal / Email)
- Running it on a cloud VM or serverless, rather than tied to your laptop
- Scheduled tasks that must run unattended
- Cross-session memory and self-accumulating skills
- Using your own endpoint or multiple providers such as OpenRouter
- Command-level approval plus DM pairing as a security boundary

**Not a fit for these four cases.**

- Coding tasks only — it is a general assistant; coding is one of many things
- Using it as an embedded SDK — it is a complete runtime, not a library
- A detailed "state vs context" layered guarantee — it has many mechanisms,
  but the vendor does not split them along those two layers

⚠ **Unknown: enterprise multi-user and audit. The vendor provides no separate documentation.**

> Checked the security and messaging pages: both cover only single-owner
> allowlist / DM pairing authorization, not multi-tenant audit.
langgraph:
**Fits**: agent flows that run long and must resume precisely from an interruption; a human stepping into the middle of a flow to change state; managing working memory and cross-session memory separately; an explicit graph structure (branches, loops, subgraphs); teams on Python.
**Not a fit**: needing built-in sandboxing or file-level permission boundaries (official docs do not provide such a mechanism — checked the README and the interrupts page); wanting a filesystem and sub-agents out of the box (go with Deep Agents, the higher-level package built on LangGraph); not wanting an extra dependency on the LangChain ecosystem — model access usually goes through it.
llamaindex:
**Fits**: bringing external data sources in for retrieval and question answering; needing one of the 300+ ready-made integrations; a Python stack; explicitly wanting LlamaParse's parsing capability (that goes through the commercial platform).

**Not a fit for**: wanting the commercial platform's managed orchestration and Agent Builder (LlamaAgents); agents that read and write files in your project directory and run commands — that is the Deep Agents "workspace filesystem" category; needing explicit sandbox and permission boundaries — the official framework docs provide no such mechanism; needing managed "keep running after shutdown" execution — that is the LlamaAgents platform side.
openai-agents-sdk:
**Fits**: you want a thin harness with built-in guardrails / human-in-the-loop, first-class MCP support, and a Python stack.
**Not a fit**: a ready-made long-task workspace (use Deep Agents or the SandboxAgent route); a TypeScript ecosystem (use openai-agents-js).
openhands:
**What it is good for**:

- Running agents 7×24 on your own server
- Scheduled or webhook triggers (Slack / GitHub / Linear / Notion)
- Managing several agents from one interface, including ACP-compatible ones such as Codex, Claude Code and Gemini
- Per-conversation container isolation
- Deploying the front end separately from the agent runtime
- Long sessions that need the official condenser to hold down context cost

**What it is not for**:

- Embedding an agent into your own Python process — use software-agent-sdk or OpenAI Agents SDK for that
- A one-off job on a single machine — it is a whole stack, not a library
- Multi-user, fine-grained permissions — the official comparison table puts Multi-user RBAC in Enterprise, so OSS self-hosting has a single key only
context7:
Scenarios needing current-version library documentation: API changes after an upgrade, configuration options introduced in a new version, usage of third-party libraries the model is unsure about.

**Not a fit for** confidential material — **queries are sent to Upstash servers, so assess data leaving your machine first.**
everything:
Scenarios where you are testing an MCP client implementation rather than using a tool.

**Not a fit for** real work — the official page states its only purpose is verifying that a client implements the protocol correctly.
fetch:
Scenarios needing to pull a web page's content as Markdown for an agent to read.

**Not a fit for** anything where reaching local or internal network addresses matters — **the official README carries an explicit security warning on exactly this point.**
filesystem:
Scenarios where an agent must read or write within explicitly declared directories.

**Not a fit for** open-ended exploration of the filesystem — allowed directories must be declared, there is no silent whole-disk access.
git:
Scenarios where an agent should make version-control operations inside a specific repository.

**Not a fit for** read-only use — full local write capability, so scope matters.
memory:
Scenarios needing cross-session memory that survives restarts and is queryable as a graph.

**Not a fit for** anything with access-control requirements — **memory is written to disk with no access control.**
playwright:
Scenarios where an agent must operate a real browser and read the page as structure rather than as a picture.

**Not a fit for** visual-only understanding — it drives the accessibility tree, so anything conveyed purely by pixels is out of reach.
sequential-thinking:
Scenarios where a complex problem benefits from being worked through step by step in a revisable, branchable way.

**Not a fit for** adding capability — **it produces structure, not intelligence.**
time:
Scenarios where an agent needs the current date and time to reason about scheduling, logs or freshness.

**Not a fit for** anything beyond time — it is one tool with one narrow purpose.
ag2:
Orchestrating **multi-agent conversations / a protocol-driven network** in Python (Hub + channels, with consulting, discussion, and workflow adapters)
Needing auditable durable messaging (write-ahead log, audit trail) and cross-process deployment (WsLink)
Running on local models (Ollama / vLLM / LM Studio)
Needing HITL and a restricted shell tool; MCP and AG-UI integration
Preferring opt-in, composable harness primitives

**Not a fit for** expecting `pip install ag2` to still be the classic AutoGen API (since v1.0 those classes live in `ag2-classic`); needing a **vendor-managed backend** (it is a pure library — you run the process); needing out-of-the-box **container-level sandboxing** (officially you get a restricted-shell allowlist, not a container); or non-Python stacks (there is no official non-Python port).
amp:
Four kinds of use fit:

- People who want an agent that **keeps working in a cloud orb after you close your laptop**
- Teams that need **multi-model frontier routing plus the Oracle second-opinion model**
- People already working in a terminal or a VS Code-family editor who want IDE integration
- Organisations needing enterprise controls (SSO, audit logs, MCP allowlists, zero data retention)

**Not a fit for** anyone who assumes tools are gated by approval — officially, "By default, Amp does not ask for approval before running tools". Approval takes a custom policy plugin that you write yourself.
continue:
**A fit for three groups:**

- People who need model freedom (many providers, including local models via Ollama) and do not want to be locked to one vendor.
- People already working in VS Code / JetBrains who want an open-source, auditable extension.
- People who want the same agent in the terminal and in CI (`cn -p`).

**Not a fit for** scenarios needing ongoing maintenance and long-term evolution — the upstream repository is read-only and the company was acquired by Cursor, so it persists only in a "code is still freely usable" form. Also not a fit for anyone relying on official support and continued fixes.
copilot-cli:
People already in the GitHub ecosystem who want to walk the whole chain from reading a repo to opening a pull request in the terminal. The official use case gives tasks such as "create a pull request on GitHub.com".

People who need scripted or headless use: `copilot -p` with approval flags is CI-friendly. Anyone who wants the MCP / plugin / custom-agent surface.

**Not a fit for** people who don't want a Copilot subscription, because the CLI ships with the subscription and cannot be bought on its own. Nor for anyone who wants "fully autonomous and zero risk": auto-approval has to be paired with an isolated environment, and the official docs warn about that plainly.
cursor-cli:
People doing engineering work in the terminal, writing scripts, or running CI/CD. The official GitHub Actions docs and cookbook cover this.
People already on Cursor who want the editor and the terminal to share one account, model set and MCP config.
People who need to hand a session to a Cloud Agent or keep it running through a persistent session.

**Not a fit** where an open-source licence or full self-hosting is required. Cursor CLI is a closed-source commercial product: it needs a Cursor account or an API key, and usage draws on the same account quota pools.
factory-droid:
End-to-end software engineering in the terminal for teams that need enterprise governance.
Particularly good for: a plan-implement-test loop on an existing repo (`/missions` multi-agent orchestration); CI/CD automation (`droid exec` one-shot runs with JSON output and a non-zero exit on failure); organizations that need BYOK, local models or airgapped deployment to avoid a single-vendor lock-in.

**Not a fit for** individuals looking for a free, lightweight terminal assistant — the lowest tier is already Pro at $20/mo, with no free plan; and `droid exec` is read-only by default, so auto-editing files requires explicitly raising the autonomy level.
github-mcp:
Anyone who wants their MCP client (VS Code, Claude Desktop, Cursor, Windsurf, Codex, Gemini CLI, etc.) to work with GitHub in natural language — reading code and repo structure, managing issues and PRs, watching Actions, triaging code-scanning / Dependabot alerts.
Users who do not want to run anything locally — pick the **remote hosted** form.
GitHub Enterprise Server users, or anyone needing self-hosted HTTP / offline-controllable setups — pick the **local** form.
Security-conscious setups that want read-only mode, toolset trimming and lockdown filtering.
goose:
**A fit for four kinds of people.**

- People who want a **local-first, general-purpose agent** that can switch to any provider — including local models — and does more than write code.
- People who need both a desktop app and a CLI.
- Organisations that want MCP extensions as the core extension surface, with an allowlist for control.
- People wiring an agent into scripts or CI (`goose run --output-format json`).

**Not a fit for** anything that has to keep running after your machine is switched off.

goose is a local process.

The non-interactive mode of `goose run` is only scripted execution — close the computer and it stops.
jules:
Self-contained, verifiable work: fixing a named bug, bumping dependencies, adding tests, migrating code snippets, small features — officially delivered as "test verified patches" and "PRs with runnable code and test results," which is exactly what makes it good for "submit the task and come back to a PR."

**Not a fit for** work that needs a live shell you can steer while it runs (CLI/IDE agents do that better), or vague, architecture-level tasks that need heavy clarification — the official FAQ itself lists "vague prompts" among the common causes of a failed task.
junie:
People already using JetBrains IDEs (IntelliJ IDEA / PyCharm / WebStorm / GoLand and more) who want an agent in the same environment.
Teams that value "plan before code" and multi-model / BYOK flexibility.
Anyone who needs the same agent in the terminal or CI/CD (Junie CLI).

**Not a fit for** users in Mainland China — the official licensing page states "Junie coding agent is not available to users in Mainland China due to regional restrictions"; nor for AI Enterprise tier users (that page states the tier does not currently include Junie), nor for anyone who needs a vendor-hosted cloud background environment.
kiro:
Teams doing formal engineering delivery in the AWS ecosystem who want specs before implementation.
People who need a cloud session that keeps running after they close the laptop (Cloud Sessions, up to 10 concurrent).
Teams that want steering and permission rules shipped with the repository (`.kiro/` is committable and consistent across surfaces).
Free tier suits low-volume trials (50 credits/month, limited to open-weight models and Claude Sonnet 4.5).

**Not a fit for** anyone who needs their own API key or local models — neither the official models page nor the pricing page documents BYOK; nor for heavy users who need a transparent quota figure, since credits are consumed by model multiplier (up to 4.4x) with no fixed request-count equivalent.
mastra:
**Fits**:

- **TypeScript / Node teams** that want an out-of-the-box agent framework - Agents, graph Workflows, Memory, RAG, Evals, MCP, a built-in server and Studio all in one package
- **Durable runs with suspend/resume** - snapshots live in your own storage and survive restarts
- **Wiring up many model providers and local models** (LMStudio is officially recommended)
- **Exposing agents and workflows over MCP**, or acting as an MCP client
- **Embedding an agent into a Next.js / React app**

**Not a fit for**:

- **A Python stack** (see [LangGraph](./langgraph.md) / [Pydantic AI](./pydantic-ai.md))
- **Wanting a low-level engine you control** - Mastra sits higher, ships a bigger package and more conventions
- **Refusing any commercial component** - platform Studio, observability and hosted deployment are separately billed, and `ee/` needs an enterprise licence
- **Needing a framework-provided process sandbox or network policy** - that part is not in the OSS core
microsoft-agent-framework:
**It is a graph-workflow orchestration framework — a fit for five cases.**

- Organizing multiple agents into a **deterministic graph workflow** with branching, human-in-the-loop, and checkpoint-based recovery
- Needing a consistent API across **.NET and Python**
- Teams already inside the Azure / Microsoft Foundry ecosystem
- Requiring observability (built-in OpenTelemetry), durability, governance, and provider flexibility
- Needing MCP and A2A cross-runtime interop, or migrating from Semantic Kernel / AutoGen

**Not a fit for** running just a single agent without a graph (OpenAI Agents SDK is lighter); needing a framework-level file or process sandbox (not provided — default permissions come from the chosen provider); wanting a stack with no Azure dependency (Ollama and Foundry Local exist, but the official hosting path is still Azure-centric); requiring a stable GA API (currently **public preview**, so breaking changes are possible).
pydantic-ai:
**A fit when:** you are a Python team that wants type-safe structured output plus dependency injection for your agents; you need to turn an agent run **durable**, using an engine you already operate; you are doing multi-agent work (delegation / hand-off / graph); you want first-class MCP support and want MCP running **locally** so you keep control of credentials; you want a thin agent loop and also want the official ready-made Harness (Coder / Researcher / memory / guardrails).
**Not a fit when:** you are on TypeScript / Node (see Mastra); you want the smallest possible dependency set and do not want to bring in Pydantic; you want to avoid every commercial component (Logfire and Gateway are official recommendations but **optional**); you need process-level sandboxing and network policy built into the framework — the sandbox lives in the Harness / Monty, not in the core SDK.
smolagents:
**Fits**: teams that buy into **code-as-action** (officially ~30% fewer steps than JSON tool calls) and are willing to sandbox LLM-generated code; anyone who needs **model-agnostic** support and local models (transformers / Ollama / mlx-lm); developers who want a thin, hackable library — Python stack; projects that want MCP / LangChain / HF Hub Space as tool sources.

**Not a fit**: needing a vendor-hosted always-on background or resumable runs — it is a pure library and memory is not persisted to disk; unwilling to take on arbitrary-code-execution risk but also unwilling to run a remote sandbox; wanting batteries-included filesystem / memory / sub-agent orchestration.
warp:
Developers who run both shell commands and coding agent work in the terminal and want team collaboration plus cloud automation. Particularly good for: teams standardizing terminal workflows as Warp Drive Workflows / Notebooks; teams delegating background work such as issue triage or PR review to cloud agents; enterprises that need SSO, data governance or self-hosted cloud agents.

**Not a fit for** people who avoid terminal agents entirely and just want a classic terminal — the Free tier works as a modern terminal, but cloud agents, Warp Drive collaboration and codebase indexing are all capped.
